    Chapter 11

    Digital Signatures: Unforgeable Digital Ink

    🤔 How can anyone on Earth check that a file came from you, without being able to forge your signature themselves?

    • ⏱️ ~5 min
    • 📚 8 sections
    • 🎮 2 interactive
    • ⭐ 200 XP
    • 🔑 1 fragment

    11.1The idea#

    A digital signature proves three things about a message or file:

    1. Who created or approved it (authentication).
    2. That it hasn't changed since it was signed (integrity).
    3. That the signer can't later deny signing it (non-repudiation).

    And unlike a MAC, anyone can verify it, using the signer's public key.

    A digital signature is much stronger than a handwritten one. A handwritten signature looks the same on every document, so it can be traced or cut and pasted. A digital signature is computed from the document's contents, so it's different for every document. Move it to another document, or change a single comma, and it no longer verifies.

    ✔ section read

    11.2How signing and verifying work#

    Why hash first? Public-key operations are slow and work on small inputs. Hashing shrinks a document of any size to 32 bytes, and the hash's collision resistance (Chapter 6) means signing the hash is as good as signing the whole document. That's also why broken hashes (MD5, SHA-1) break signatures: if Mallory can find two documents with the same hash, a signature on one is valid for the other.

    ⚠️ You'll often hear "a signature is the hash encrypted with the private key." That's roughly true for RSA, but not for ECDSA or Ed25519, which use different math. The intuition that matters: only the private key can create the signature, and the public key can check it.

    11.4Hash vs. MAC vs. signature#

    Hash MAC Digital signature
    Key None One shared secret key Private key signs, public key verifies
    Detects accidental changes ✅ ✅ ✅
    Detects deliberate tampering ❌ (attacker can recompute) ✅ ✅
    Proves who made it ❌ ✅ (to the other key holder only) ✅ (to anyone)
    Non-repudiation ❌ ❌ ✅
    Speed Fastest Very fast Slower
    Example SHA-256 HMAC-SHA256 Ed25519, ECDSA, RSA-PSS
    ✔ section read

    11.5Signature algorithms#

    Algorithm Based on Public key Signature Status and notes
    RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 Factoring 256–512 B 256–512 B ⚠️ Very common in certificates; acceptable for signatures
    RSA-PSS Factoring 256–512 B 256–512 B ✅ Preferred RSA signature; used by TLS 1.3
    DSA Discrete log — — ❌ Obsolete
    ECDSA (P-256) Elliptic curves 64 B ~64–72 B ✅ Very common (TLS certificates, passkeys). ⚠️ Needs a perfect random number for every signature.
    Ed25519 (EdDSA) Curve25519 32 B 64 B ✅ Recommended: fast, small, deterministic, hard to misuse
    Schnorr (secp256k1) Elliptic curves 32 B 64 B ✅ Used by Bitcoin since the 2021 "Taproot" upgrade
    ML-DSA (Dilithium) Lattices ~1.3–2.6 KB ~2.4–4.6 KB ✅ Post-quantum standard (FIPS 204, 2024)
    SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) Hash functions only 32–64 B ~8–50 KB ✅ Post-quantum, very conservative (FIPS 205, 2024)
    FN-DSA (Falcon) Lattices ~0.9–1.8 KB ~0.7–1.3 KB Post-quantum; standard being finalized

    📜 Remember the PlayStation 3? ECDSA needs a secret random number (called a "nonce," k) for each signature. Sony used the same k every time. With two signatures made with the same k, simple algebra reveals the private key. Ed25519 avoids this entirely by computing k deterministically from the private key and the message, so there's no random number to get wrong. (A standard called RFC 6979 does the same for ECDSA.)

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Signature algorithms

    ⚠️ Legacy
    RSA PKCS#1 v1.5

    Classic RSA signatures

    • Universal in certificates
    • No security proof; big signatures
    Best for: Existing certificate chains
    ✅ Use it
    RSA-PSS

    Modern RSA signatures

    • Provable security; TLS 1.3
    • 256–512-byte signatures
    • Slow signing
    Best for: Where RSA is required
    ❌ Avoid
    DSA

    Discrete-log signatures

    • Historic standard
    • Obsolete; nonce-reuse fragile
    Best for: Nowhere
    ✅ Use it
    ECDSA P-256

    Elliptic-curve DSA

    • Small, fast, in every secure chip
    • Passkeys and certificates
    • Needs a perfect random nonce per signature (PS3!)
    • Use RFC 6979 deterministic nonces
    Best for: TLS certs, passkeys, hardware
    ✅ Use it
    Ed25519

    EdDSA on Curve25519

    • Deterministic: no nonce to get wrong
    • 32-byte keys, 64-byte signatures, very fast
    • Not in some older hardware/FIPS stacks
    Best for: SSH, Git, software signing, new designs
    👍 Situational
    Schnorr (secp256k1)

    Bitcoin Taproot

    • Simple, provable, aggregatable
    • Ecosystem mostly crypto-currency
    Best for: Bitcoin multisig
    ✅ Use it
    ML-DSA (Dilithium)

    Lattice, FIPS 204

    • Quantum-resistant
    • Fast signing and verifying
    • ~2.4–4.6 KB signatures
    • Young in production
    Best for: Post-quantum signatures
    👍 Situational
    SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+)

    Hash-based, FIPS 205

    • Relies only on hash functions: very conservative
    • Tiny public keys
    • 8–50 KB signatures
    • Slow signing
    Best for: Firmware and long-lived roots
    👍 Situational
    FN-DSA (Falcon)

    Compact lattice signatures

    • Smallest post-quantum lattice signatures
    • Floating-point math is hard to implement safely
    • Standard still being finalized
    Best for: Bandwidth-tight PQ use

    11.6Where signatures are used#

    Signatures are everywhere, mostly invisible:

    Where What's signed
    HTTPS certificates A certificate authority signs each website's certificate (Chapter 13)
    TLS handshakes The server signs the handshake to prove it owns the certificate's private key (Chapter 14)
    Software updates Windows, macOS, iOS, Android and Linux only install updates signed by the vendor
    App stores and code signing Apps must be signed (Apple notarization, Windows Authenticode, Android APK signing)
    Package managers Linux apt/dnf packages; npm, PyPI and container images increasingly use signing services such as Sigstore
    Git Signed commits and tags prove who wrote the code
    Documents PDF signatures, electronic signature services, legally recognized digital signatures (e.g. under EU eIDAS)
    Passports The chip in an ePassport holds your data signed by the issuing country
    Email DKIM signatures prove an email really came from the sending domain (Chapter 16)
    DNS DNSSEC signs DNS records (Chapter 15)
    Cryptocurrency Every transaction is signed with the owner's private key (Chapter 16)
    Web tokens JWTs signed with RS256, ES256 or EdDSA (Chapter 16)
    Secure Boot Each stage of startup checks the signature of the next, from firmware to operating system
    Passkeys Your device signs a login challenge (Chapter 16)
    ✔ section read

    11.7The missing piece: whose key is it?#

    A valid signature proves the message was signed by whoever holds that private key. But how do you know that a public key really belongs to Alice, or to your bank, rather than to Mallory pretending to be them?

    That question, linking keys to real identities, is what certificates and PKI solve. It's the subject of Part III.

    ✔ section read

    11.8Hands-on with signatures#

    🧪 Try it yourself (OpenSSL, Ed25519):

    Terminal
    # Generate a signing key pair
openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out signer.pem
openssl pkey -in signer.pem -pubout -out signer_pub.pem

# Sign a document
echo "I, Alice, owe Bob 10 dollars." > contract.txt
openssl pkeyutl -sign -inkey signer.pem -rawin -in contract.txt -out contract.sig
ls -l contract.sig          # 64 bytes

# Anyone with the PUBLIC key can verify
openssl pkeyutl -verify -pubin -inkey signer_pub.pem -rawin \
  -in contract.txt -sigfile contract.sig
# Signature Verified Successfully

# Now someone tampers with the contract...
echo "I, Alice, owe Bob 1000 dollars." > contract.txt
openssl pkeyutl -verify -pubin -inkey signer_pub.pem -rawin \
  -in contract.txt -sigfile contract.sig
# Signature Verification Failure

    With RSA (the classic way to sign files such as software releases):

    Terminal
    echo "release v1.0" > release.txt
openssl dgst -sha256 -sign alice_private.pem -out release.sig release.txt
openssl dgst -sha256 -verify alice_public.pem -signature release.sig release.txt
# Verified OK

    In Python:

    Python
    from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ed25519 import Ed25519PrivateKey
from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidSignature

signing_key = Ed25519PrivateKey.generate()
verify_key  = signing_key.public_key()       # share this one

document  = b"I, Alice, owe Bob $10."
signature = signing_key.sign(document)       # 64 bytes

verify_key.verify(signature, document)        # no exception → valid
print("valid")

try:
    verify_key.verify(signature, b"I, Alice, owe Bob $1000.")
except InvalidSignature:
    print("forgery detected")

    Real-world example: verifying a Linux download. Remember the SHA256SUMS file from Chapter 6? Ubuntu also publishes SHA256SUMS.gpg, a signature of that file. After importing Ubuntu's public signing key (obtained from a trusted source), you run:

    Terminal
    gpg --verify SHA256SUMS.gpg SHA256SUMS     # is the checksum list genuine?
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing    # does my download match it?

    Now a hacker who replaces the download and the checksum still fails, because they can't forge Ubuntu's signature.
